datasets.name: Gapminder — life expectancy, population & GDP
datasets.description: Country-level life expectancy, population and GDP per capita for 142 countries, 1952-2007. The classic development dataset.

datasets.name: Our World in Data — life expectancy
datasets.description: Long-run life expectancy at birth for every country, some series reaching back to the 1700s. Tidy CSV straight from the OWID grapher.

datasets.name: Our World in Data — COVID-19 dataset
datasets.description: Daily cases, deaths, testing, hospitalisation and vaccination for every country over the whole pandemic. Large but tidy.

datasets.name: NHANES — US national health & nutrition survey
datasets.description: Individual-level body measurements, demographics, lifestyle and lab results from the CDC's national health examination survey.

datasets.name: CDC — leading causes of death in the US
datasets.description: Age-adjusted death rates for the ten leading causes of death, by US state and year, from the National Center for Health Statistics.

datasets.name: FRED — Federal Reserve economic data
datasets.description: Hundreds of thousands of US and international macroeconomic time series: rates, inflation, employment, money supply. Pick any series that catches your eye.

access.hint: install.packages('fredr'); fredr::fredr('UNRATE')  # free API key, or CSV export from the site

datasets.name: Daily stock & index prices (Yahoo Finance)
datasets.description: Open/high/low/close/volume for any listed ticker or index, decades deep, one function call away.

datasets.name: CoinGecko — cryptocurrency market histories
datasets.description: Price, market cap and volume histories for thousands of cryptocurrencies via a free, keyless JSON API.

datasets.name: World Bank — World Development Indicators
datasets.description: 1,400+ annual indicators (GDP, poverty, education, energy, trade) for every country since 1960, queryable from R.

datasets.name: Eurostat — official EU statistics
datasets.description: The EU's statistical office: demographics, economy, agriculture, tourism, transport and more, at country and regional (NUTS) level.

datasets.name: UCI — online retail transactions
datasets.description: Half a million real transactions from a UK online giftware retailer over two years: invoices, products, quantities, prices, customer country.

access.hint: Download the xlsx from the UCI repository, then readxl::read_excel()

datasets.name: Olist — Brazilian e-commerce orders
datasets.description: 100k orders from a Brazilian marketplace: order items, payments, reviews, sellers and customer geolocation across eight relational tables.

access.hint: Download from Kaggle (free account), then read the CSVs with readr

datasets.name: UN Comtrade — international trade flows
datasets.description: Bilateral imports and exports by commodity between all countries — the canonical who-sells-what-to-whom dataset.

access.hint: install.packages('comtradr'); comtradr::ct_get_data(reporter='GB', partner='all')  # free API key

datasets.name: UN General Assembly voting records
datasets.description: Every UN General Assembly roll-call vote since 1946: country, vote, and issue classification. Great for alignment and bloc analysis.

datasets.name: MIT Election Lab — US presidential returns by county
datasets.description: County-level US presidential election results 2000-2020, with party and candidate vote counts.

access.hint: Download CSV from the Harvard Dataverse, then readr::read_csv()

datasets.name: V-Dem — Varieties of Democracy indices
datasets.description: 450+ expert-coded indicators of democracy (elections, civil liberties, media freedom) for nearly every country back to 1789.

datasets.name: UCDP/PRIO — armed conflict dataset
datasets.description: Every armed conflict since 1946 with parties, location, intensity and year — the standard academic conflict dataset.

access.hint: Download CSV from ucdp.uu.se/downloads, then readr::read_csv()

datasets.name: UNHCR — refugee population statistics
datasets.description: Refugees, asylum seekers and internally displaced people by origin and asylum country, yearly since 1951, via UNHCR's own R package.

datasets.name: NASA GISTEMP — global temperature anomalies
datasets.description: Monthly global and zonal surface temperature anomalies since 1880, maintained by NASA GISS.

datasets.name: WRI — global power plant database
datasets.description: ~35,000 power plants worldwide with location, fuel type, capacity and estimated generation.

access.hint: Download CSV from WRI / datasets.wri.org, then readr::read_csv()

datasets.name: Palmer Station penguins
datasets.description: Body measurements for 344 penguins of three species from the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica. The friendlier iris.

datasets.name: nycflights13 — every flight out of NYC in 2013
datasets.description: 336,776 flights from the three New York airports with delays, carriers, weather and plane metadata in five relational tables.

datasets.name: State of the Union addresses (full text)
datasets.description: The complete text of every US State of the Union address since 1790 — two centuries of political language in one package.

datasets.name: Spotify songs — audio features of 30k tracks
datasets.description: Danceability, energy, valence, tempo and popularity for ~30,000 songs across six genres (TidyTuesday, sourced from the Spotify API).

datasets.name: International football results, 1872-present
datasets.description: Every men's international football match since 1872: teams, score, tournament, venue. 47k+ matches, updated continuously.

datasets.name: TidyTuesday lucky dip
datasets.description: Let fate go one level deeper: pick a random week from the TidyTuesday archive of 300+ curated, pre-cleaned datasets and use whatever you get.

questions.template: What is the long-run trend in {dataset}? Decompose it: how much is secular drift, how much is seasonal or cyclical, and how much is noise?
Find the moment the story changed in {dataset}. Is there a structural break or regime change, and what real-world event coincides with it?
Build a forecast from {dataset} for the next few periods. Compare a naive baseline against a proper model — how much does the model actually buy you?
Are countries in {dataset} converging or diverging over time? Quantify the gap between the top and bottom groups and how it has moved.
Run a PCA on {dataset}. What do the first two or three components mean in plain language, and which observations sit far from everyone else?
Cluster the observations in {dataset}. How many natural groups are there, do they match any existing labels, and what defines each group?
Hunt for anomalies in {dataset}. Define "unusual" quantitatively, flag the strangest observations, and investigate whether they are errors or stories.
Map {dataset}. Is the spatial pattern clustered, dispersed, or random — and can you back that judgement with a statistic rather than a glance?
Build a choropleth (or point map) from {dataset} that tells one clear story, then write the three-sentence caption that a newspaper would print.
Treat {dataset} as a network. Who are the most central nodes, does the network have communities, and how has its structure shifted over time?
Build a defensible ranking from {dataset}. Who is top, who is bottom, how sensitive is the ordering to your methodological choices?
Pick two variables in {dataset} that correlate strongly. Argue both sides: what would the causal story be, and what confounder could explain it away?
Study the full distribution in {dataset}, not just the mean. How skewed or unequal is it (Gini, top-decile share), and is that concentration growing?
Take one headline number you can compute from {dataset} and put honest uncertainty around it using bootstrap or permutation methods. Does the headline survive?
Profile the missing data in {dataset}. Is it missing at random? Who or what is systematically absent, and how would that bias a naive analysis?
Track sentiment and emotional language across {dataset} over time. When was the tone darkest, and does it track historical events?
Fit a topic model to {dataset}. What themes emerge, and how has their prominence risen and fallen across the corpus?
Isolate the seasonal or weekly rhythm in {dataset}. What repeats, how strong is the cycle, and is the rhythm itself changing?
Split {dataset} into meaningful cohorts and compare them. Which difference between groups is largest, and does it hold up after controlling for an obvious confounder?
The interesting answer in {dataset} needs at least two of its tables. Find a question that only a join can answer, and answer it.

challenges.name: No tidyverse
challenges.description: Do the whole analysis and all plots in base R — no dplyr, no ggplot2. Rediscover aggregate(), tapply() and friends.

challenges.name: One pipe to rule them all
challenges.description: Express the core data transformation as a single unbroken pipe chain, from raw data to plot-ready table.

challenges.name: Make it interactive
challenges.description: Deliver the result as an interactive graphic (plotly, ggiraph or leaflet) with tooltips that genuinely add information.

challenges.name: Ship a dashboard
challenges.description: Present the findings as a Quarto dashboard with at least three coordinated panels.

challenges.name: The chart stands alone
challenges.description: Produce one chart so thoroughly annotated (title, subtitle, direct labels, source note) that it needs no surrounding text at all.

challenges.name: Colour with care
challenges.description: Use only a colourblind-safe palette (viridis or Okabe-Ito) and verify the result with a simulator before calling it done.

challenges.name: Bring a friend
challenges.description: Join in a second dataset from this generator's own index and make the combination essential to the answer.

challenges.name: 100 lines, max
challenges.description: The entire analysis — import to final figure — in at most 100 lines of R, comments included.

challenges.name: Speak data.table
challenges.description: Use data.table for every transformation instead of your usual tools, idiomatically (no dplyr translations).

challenges.name: Package it
challenges.description: Wrap the core logic as functions in a minimal R package with roxygen docs and at least three testthat tests.

challenges.name: Small multiples, no legends
challenges.description: Every comparison must be a faceted small-multiples chart with direct labelling — legends are banned.

challenges.name: Newsroom style
challenges.description: Style the final graphic like The Economist, FT or BBC — typography, grid, annotations and all — using a theme you build yourself.

challenges.name: Reproducible pipeline
challenges.description: Orchestrate the analysis with the {targets} package so a single tar_make() rebuilds everything from scratch.

challenges.name: No loops
challenges.description: No for or while loops anywhere — vectorised operations and purrr/apply functions only.

challenges.name: The table is the chart
challenges.description: Make a beautifully formatted table (gt or reactable) the centrepiece deliverable instead of a plot.

challenges.name: Publish it in webR
challenges.description: Publish the analysis so it runs in the reader's browser via webR or shinylive — just like this generator does.

challenges.name: Tell it in five slides
challenges.description: Condense the whole project into five presentation slides (Quarto revealjs) a non-technical audience could follow.

challenges.name: Defend your axes
challenges.description: Somewhere a log scale, index (=100) rebasing, or per-capita adjustment changes the story. Show the naive version and the adjusted one, and argue for your choice.

challenges.name: Stress-test it
challenges.description: Identify the three most consequential analytical choices you made and show how the headline result moves when each is varied.

challenges.name: Data art
challenges.description: Alongside the serious analysis, render the same data as a purely aesthetic generative-art piece.
